Abstract
A method is disclosed to fabricate a Palladium cathode that can be electrolyzed in heavy water and stimulated with a laser at a predetermined wavelength to produce apparent excess power; the fabrication method involves cold working, polishing, etching and annealing the Palladium prior to electrolytic loading with Deuterium. Loading is accomplished with the cathode sitting in a magnetic field of 350 Gauss. After loading the cathode with Deuterium, Gold is co-deposited electrolytically on the cathode. When a coating of Gold is visible on the cathode, co-deposition is halted and the cathode is stimulated with a low-power laser with a maximum power of 30 milliwatts. The thermal response of the cathode is typically 500 mW with maximum output observed of approximately 1 watt. The effect is repeatable when protocols are followed and has been demonstrated in several laboratories.
Overview
Dennis Letts and Dennis Cravens describe a protocol for producing apparent excess power from a palladium cathode electrolysed in heavy water and illuminated by a low-power laser, presented at the Tenth International Conference on Cold Fusion in 2003.
The preparation is specified in detail. The palladium is cold-worked, polished, etched and annealed before electrolytic loading with deuterium, and the loading is carried out with the cathode sitting in a 350 gauss magnetic field. Gold is then co-deposited electrolytically onto the cathode, and the co-deposition is halted once a gold coating is visible.
The stimulation is optical. The prepared cathode is illuminated with a low-power laser of at most 30 milliwatts, at a wavelength the authors describe as predetermined. The reported thermal response is typically 500 mW, with a maximum observed output of about 1 watt.

Lester Jennings Hendershot (3 June 1898 – 19 April 1961) was an American inventor , best known for the so-called Hendershot fuelless generator (or "Fuelless Motor"), a device he unveiled in 1928 that he claimed produced electrical power without any fuel. The invention drew national press attention and the interest of prominent backers before commercial and political difficulties led Hendershot to abandon it. Its operation was never explained or independently verified, and its claimed fuelless output is not accepted by mainstream science.
Education
Attended Cornell University briefly, taking a few courses; he earned no degree, and his formal schooling was limited.
Biography
Lester Hendershot was born on 3 June 1898 in West Elizabeth, Pennsylvania. He had little formal education and was largely self-taught as an inventor, achieving modest success with electronic toys and selling some of his ideas to small manufacturers.
In the 1920s, while working on a new type of fuelless aviation compass, Hendershot reported that he had stumbled upon a method of generating electrical energy. He developed this into what he called a "magnetic induction" motor, first announced in March 1928. The device — quickly dubbed a "fuelless motor" by the press — attracted intense publicity and the attention of well-known figures, including Major Thomas Lanphier, commandant at Selfridge Field, and Henry Breckinridge, the attorney for Colonel Charles Lindbergh, who was among those said to have taken an interest in the invention.

Marko Rodin is an American independent researcher and inventor, the originator of Vortex-Based Mathematics (VBM) and of the toroidal winding pattern known as the Rodin coil . The coil is among the most widely replicated devices in the amateur new energy community, and a substantial body of experimental reports on it is catalogued on this wiki.
Origin of Vortex-Based Mathematics
By Rodin's own account, the number system did not begin as a physics investigation but as a religious inquiry . Raised in the Bahá'í Faith , he set out to find what he took to be the precise mystical significance of the Most Great Name of God, and converted its superlative form Abhá into numbers using the Abjad system, in which each letter of the Arabic alphabet carries a numerical value. Taking A = 1, b = 2, h = 5, á = 1, the letters sum to 9 — a number given repeated significance in Bahá'í scripture. From that starting point he developed the patterns he came to call Vortex-Based Mathematics.
This origin is worth stating plainly because it explains the structure of the system, which is organised throughout around the number 9 and around digit sums. It should also be said that VBM is not Bahá'í doctrine and carries no standing within that religion, which cautions against numerology.
Vortex-Based Mathematics
The system works in modulo-9 arithmetic : every number is reduced by repeatedly summing its digits until a single value from 1 to 9 remains. Two features are then treated as fundamental.
The first is the doubling sequence . Repeatedly doubling and reducing gives 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 7 (16) → 5 (32) → 1 (64), a closed six-step loop; halving traverses the same loop in reverse. Rodin identifies this circuit with what he calls "the longest free-flowing path of the electron", and the coil is wound to follow it.

Abstract
Two mechanisms utilized to explain the operation of railguns are explained: one based on Ampere's force and the other on the transfer of momentum through electromagnetic waves. It is shown how the former is compatible with the data while the latter has problems with the quantitative figures and the case of the immobilized projectile.
Overview
On the Mechanism of Railguns is a three-page paper by Andre K T Assis of the Department of Cosmic Rays and Chronology at the State University of Campinas, published in Galilean Electrodynamics volume 3, number 5 (September/October 1992), pages 93–95.
It compares two accounts of what accelerates a railgun projectile. In a railgun, current from a source flows out along one fixed rail, across a conducting projectile bridging the rails, and back along the other; a ponderomotive force drives the projectile along the rails. Assis asks where that force comes from.
The first candidate is Ampère's force law, the 1820s expression for the force between two current elements, which he gives as his equation (1). The second, advanced by Pappas and others, is that momentum is transferred by the reflection of electromagnetic waves from the projectile, with a backward-propagating radiation field carrying the recoil.
Assis argues for the first on three grounds. Ampère's law satisfies Newton's third law "in the strongest form," so that a closed circuit cannot exert a net force on itself — consistent with the fact that no experiment has demonstrated such a bootstrap effect in metallic circuits. Perpetual Motion: The History of an Obsession is a history of perpetual-motion machines and the people who built them, by the English mechanical and aeronautical engineer Arthur W J G Ord-Hume . First published by George Allen & Unwin in London in 1977 , with 235 pages and 95 illustrations, it has stayed in print through several reissues and is generally treated as the standard work on its subject.
It is an unusual entry in this collection, because it is a sceptical book. Ord-Hume's subject is a four-century record of failure, and his thesis is that the failures mattered: "without their early experiments the science of mechanics would not have developed so rapidly."
The argument
The book takes the proposition at its plainest — "make a machine which gives out more work than the energy you put into it and you have perpetual motion" — and follows its pursuit from the medieval overbalancing wheel to the twentieth century.
Two threads run through it. The first is how the impossibility was established : the attempts, and the increasingly precise reasons for their failure, are part of how mechanics arrived at the conservation laws. The inventors were, in Ord-Hume's account, the unwitting experimental arm of a science that had not yet been formulated, and the basic tenets of engineering grew out of their defeats .
The second is the character of the pursuit, which the subtitle names. Ord-Hume is interested in why the problem grips people — and he distinguishes carefully between the self-deceived, the merely mistaken, and the outright frauds , of whom there were many. The tone is neither credulous nor contemptuous.

Peter Grandics is a Hungarian-born chemical and biochemical engineer based in Carlsbad, California, who has worked in biomedical research and, more recently, on atmospheric energy harvesting.
Education

Work
Grandics spent most of his career in biomedical research and bioseparation technology before turning to energy. His 2007 paper " The Pyramidal Electric Transducer ", published in Infinite Energy , proposes that the global atmospheric electric circuit could be tapped for commercial power by a conducting pyramid acting as a wideband antenna for electrostatic discharge impulses, coupled to a lumped-element resonant circuit that converts random impulses into damped sinusoidal wave trains.
The paper combines bench measurements — swept-signal analyses of the coil system, differential measurements of energy transfer between primary and secondary windings, and discharge trains driven by a laboratory Van de Graaff generator — with an argument that the dimensional ratios of the Great Pyramid of Giza encode both sine-wave parameters and the golden ratio, and that the structure may therefore have been designed as an antenna. He holds patents on the transducer design and presented the work at the ExtraOrdinary Technology Conference in 2009.
The engineering claim rests on the available power in the atmospheric circuit, which is the point on which it is usually assessed: the global circuit carries roughly a kiloampere at about 250 kV, a total of some 250 megawatts spread over the whole Earth.

Roberto Blas is an Argentine physicist at the Universidad Nacional de Río Cuarto in Córdoba, working on the electrodynamics of homopolar machines.
His published work is a collaboration with Jorge A Guala-Valverde of the Fundación Julio Palacios in Neuquén, and in most cases with Max Blas as a third author. The programme is experimental: it uses Faraday-disc and homopolar motor-generator arrangements to ask what determines the electromotive force in a rotating magnetic system — motion relative to the magnet, relative to the field-shaping iron, or relative to the laboratory. The group's distinctive apparatus is the "confined B-field" machine described in Non-Local Motional EM Induction (2005), in which an iron yoke channels a rotatable magnet's flux into a narrow air gap, so that magnet, yoke and coil can each be held or spun independently.
The interpretation the group favours is a relational one drawing on Weber electrodynamics and on Amperian surface currents, and the same theme runs through their other papers: "Inertial Mass: a Changing Entity? Weber vs. Einstein, Weber Plus Einstein or None?" (2005), "Maxwell Helps Explain Microphysics" (2002), and "Non-Local Motional Electrodynamics" (2009). Guala-Valverde's related work on homopolar induction has also appeared in the American Journal of Physics and Physica Scripta .

What the record stands for
Schauberger wrote in German and published very little in English during his lifetime. The English-speaking alternative-energy community of the 1970s and 1980s therefore depended on a small number of translators, and this record marks one of those efforts.
The World Science Database entry (abstract record 3867) gives the year as 1988 and the journal as Causes , with no volume, page range or article titles. The 1988–1991 span comes from the abstract text itself rather than from any bibliographic field, so the single date shown in most listings understates the series.

Causes was a small-circulation newsletter published from Albuquerque, New Mexico , the city the World Science Database gives as Baumgartner's own. Stanley Allen Meyer (24 August 1940 – 20 March 1998) was an American independent inventor from Grove City, Ohio, known for the Water Fuel Cell — a device he said could split water into hydrogen and oxygen using far less electrical energy than conventional electrolysis requires, so that a vehicle could run on water alone. He fitted the apparatus to a dune buggy, demonstrated it publicly from 1986 onwards, and held a series of United States patents on the components.
Meyer's claim was that the cell dissociated water not by brute-force current but by voltage — a high-voltage pulse train applied to a resonant cavity, drawing negligible current. He called the sequence the Hydrogen Fracturing Process . If it worked as described, the energy released by burning the resulting gas would exceed the energy used to produce it, which is why the claim attracted both wide attention and the flat rejection of the physics community.
In 1996 an Ohio court, hearing a suit brought by two investors, found that the cell was performing ordinary electrolysis and ruled that Meyer had committed "gross and egregious fraud". He died two years later, at 57, of a ruptured cerebral aneurysm; his reported dying words — "they poisoned me" — have kept the circumstances in dispute among his supporters ever since, though the coroner's finding and a three-month police investigation found no evidence of foul play.

In 2003, Heins filed a patent application in Canada[1] although the patent application is now "dead".[2] Heins also founded Potential Difference Inc, the website of which contains a series of videos of the inventor demonstrating the machine.[3] Heins has recently stated that he is unsure whether or not the machine really produces energy, but in communications with science writer David Bradley of ScienceBase, Heins made claims of up to 7000% efficiency for a bi-toroidal transformer.[4] Heins, who reportedly works 8–12 hours a day on the Perepiteia, insists that it is viable and that "This technology should be mainstream."

Overview
The book argues for a continuity between the aims of historical alchemy and certain strands of twentieth-century physics, on the premise that both were concerned with altering the constitution of matter itself rather than merely rearranging it. Farrell's method throughout is to read alchemical texts as descriptions of a physical medium, and then to look for modern counterparts to what he takes them to describe.
Three lines of material are drawn together. The first is the claim, associated with David Hudson, that the platinum-group metals can exist in a monatomic or "high spin" state with anomalous properties — the substance often called monatomic gold. The second is Soviet and Russian work, principally that of the astrophysicist Nikolai A Kozyrev on rotation, time and what later writers termed torsion physics, together with the "red mercury" legend that circulated after the collapse of the Soviet Union. The third is Farrell's continuing subject: German wartime research, here the device known as Die Glocke ("the Bell") and the substance identified in that literature as "Serum 525," approached alongside isotope enrichment and laser work.
The Bell and the wartime material connect this book to its predecessor, Secrets of the Unified Field: The Philadelphia Experiment, The Nazi Bell, and the Discarded Theory (2008), which treats the same device in relation to Einstein's abandoned unified field theory.

This problem is, of course, trivial and boring; the particle just sits there. The next simplest problem, a toy universe of two, classical, charged particles, is both nontrivial and unsolved! There are, however, approximation techniques, so that practical problems can be mastered. Then it in turn is taken as a current, its EM fields are calculated at the position of the first, where then Lor-entz's force law gives a perturbation-correction. This is then continued back and forth until an approximation of the desired accuracy is obtained. But, to date, there is no widely-accepted closed formulation for the dynamics of such a toy universe. Reed claimed to have built a motor driven entirely by permanent magnets that consumed no fuel and produced no emissions. According to accounts of his demonstrations, an early 1989 prototype stood about seven feet tall, weighed more than 500 pounds, had four moving parts, and was said to power a 500-watt generator. He described the mechanism as a horizontal shaft carrying magnets, with spring-loaded, magnet-tipped pistons above it whose motion was claimed to sustain the shaft's rotation once started by hand crank.
Reed said later versions were much smaller — reportedly about 20 inches high and under 200 pounds — and that they could drive a 7,000-watt generator, enough, he claimed, to power an average home. He also said he had built a car called the "Surge" that used his motor technology and recharged itself while being driven rather than needing to be plugged in.

Vladimir Georgievich Kadyshevsky (5 May 1937 – 24 September 2014) was a Russian theoretical physicist, an Academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and Director of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research at Dubna from 1992 to 2005. He worked on quantum field theory and elementary particle theory, and is remembered for two things in particular: the three-dimensional relativistic scattering equation that carries his name, and a long programme to modify quantum field theory by introducing a fundamental mass — an upper limit to the mass spectrum, standing to the mass scale as the velocity of light stands to velocity.
He appears on this wiki as an editor of The Lorentz Group, CPT and Neutrinos (2001) and as the author of " A New High Energy Scale ", the paper in which he set out the fundamental-mass programme to the Frontiers of Fundamental Physics conference at Olympia in 1993.
Biography
Kadyshevsky was born in Moscow on 5 May 1937. From 1946 to 1954 he attended the Suvorov Military School in Sverdlovsk, graduating with highest distinction, and entered the Physics Department of Lomonosov Moscow State University.

Walt Jenkins (also given as Walter P. Jenkins ) is an American independent inventor, based in Florida, who develops on-board systems intended to let internal combustion engines run largely on water. His work is marketed under the name H2G through his company H2 Global, LLC. Jenkins is a familiar figure in the independent-energy community and has been described within it as a modern successor to Stanley Meyer; his central claim is that his process is not electrolysis and does not derive from prior water-fuel art.
Biography
Jenkins came to energy research from an unrelated technical career. He has said that he worked in the motion picture industry in Hollywood during the 1970s, where he developed an early virtual set system and other computer-based production tools, and that he managed a broadcast television station in the Orlando, Florida market during the late 1990s.
He began experimenting with alternative fuel systems for cars as a hobby in the mid-1980s. By the early 2000s he was working on hydrogen extraction from water by electrolysis, and he is credited within the HHO community as the original developer of the "dry cell" electrolyser design that many later experimenters adopted. He subsequently abandoned electrolysis, saying it could never return enough fuel energy for the electrical power it consumed, and moved to a different approach.
His company H2 Global, LLC is registered in Florida and also trades online as H2GE and H4Gas. He has conducted demonstrations for accredited investors near Sarasota, Florida, and has shown a water-fuelled dune buggy on Anna Maria Island.

The World Institute for Scientific Exploration ( WISE ) is an American non-profit research organisation based in Baltimore, Maryland , incorporated in that state as a 501(c)(3) charitable corporation. Its stated purpose is to conduct and promote research on subjects that fall outside conventional funding — complementary and traditional medicine, and energy medicine in particular; new and low-cost forms of energy; consciousness and parapsychology; unidentified aerial phenomena; and unexplained phenomena generally — and to apply the results to the development of devices and services in biomedicine, energy, agriculture and the environment.
Its president and chief executive is the physician John H. Reed , who is also its treasurer.
Organisation
WISE is structured into a large number of small divisions grouped under four headings:
Earth Sciences — agriculture, earth sciences and energy
Health and Medical — eight divisions, among them behavioural medicine, nutrition and the traditional medical systems
Humanities — thirteen divisions, including archaeology, history, philosophy and religion
Science and Technology — ten divisions, including astronomy, chemistry, engineering and physics
The breadth is deliberate and is the organisation's most distinctive feature: it is not a single-subject body but an umbrella intended to cover anomalous research of any kind. Reed heads the Health and Medicine division in addition to the presidency.
